newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia rigidity drawback to investors - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia rigidity drawback to investors - analysts.

text.p: The rigid attitude of Slovenian authorities is a key obstacle for foreign investors, but the situation should improve as the country forges closer links with the European Union, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The attitude of state bodies towards foreign investment is a problem," Danilo Grasic, head of investment at the Slovenian branch of Austria's Creditanstalt, told reporters during a foreign investment conference in the northern resort of Bled.

Grasic said the negative attitude was expected to change as Slovenia moved closer to the EU. The country signed an association agreement with the EU in June and expects to become a full member by 2001.
"Most changes will come because of the orientation towards the EU," Grasic added.

Analysts said the country's mass privatisation process should help to create more opportunities for foreign direct and portfolio investors. Around 700 Slovenian companies have been fully privatised so far, while a further 1,266 selloffs are in process and are expected to be completed next year.
Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek on Tuesday said he expected a strong increase in foreign investment over the next two years as the privatisation process draws to a close.

"Government officials have repeatedly stated that foreign capital is welcome and that foreign investment will be supported," Gustav Wurmbock, managing director of the European Privatisation and Investment Corporation, said.

Slovenian law currently permits foreigners to own only a minority share in most companies, while foreign banks can establish their subsidiaries in Slovenia only after laying out substantial amounts of capital.
At the same time, cross-border transfers are burdened by complicated bureaucratic procedures and red tape.

But while it may take time to change bureaucratic routines, the listing of a batch of recently privatised companies on Ljubljana's fledgling bourse could provide at least a short-term boost to foreign investment, experts said.
"There is big interest in Slovenian shares. Foreigners are impatiently waiting for new listings of newly privatised companies," said Drasko Veselinovic, head of the Ljubljana bourse.
He added that up to 15 newly privatised firms could be listed on the primary or OTC markets of the Ljubljana bourse by the end of the year.
Foreign direct investment in Slovenia last year rose to around $150 million, or 0.8 percent of the country's gross domestic product, from $83.7 million in 1994.
